title: The column sings through its last night in the open
summary: On the bank and in the thorn below Muileann ghlas the column keeps its last night before the battle by singing low, company after company, in part for what courage it lends and in part because there are children on the field with nowhere else on the island to be left.

title: Owen Barrow walks the line before first light
summary: In the last hour of dark Owen Barrow goes the length of the column's line, speaking to each company and to many of the column by name; he is remembered in the north to have said that the hills lie behind them now and cannot be walked back to before the guns find them either way. The open record names him nowhere.

title: The guns find the thorn stand
summary: The third regiment's four field pieces, hauled the last two miles by hand through ground too soft for the horses, find the column's thorn-stand line within the first half-hour of the fighting; what holds after that holds along the bank itself, hand to hand, through most of the short forenoon.

title: The corporal's list at the mill
summary: A corporal of the third regiment draws up the regiments' dead of the day at a trestle table in the mill at Muileann ghlas, the miller's own ledger turned backward for want of other paper: three-and-twenty names, each with a town and, where known, an age.

title: A requisition for lime
summary: The regiments' burial parties ask the quartermaster for a good deal more lime than three-and-twenty graves would need. The requisition survives where no count of the column's own dead does, and is the nearest thing the open record holds to one.

title: The miller's wife keeps her kitchen through the battle
summary: As the mill at Muileann ghlas changes hands twice before noon, the miller's wife will not leave her own kitchen for either army, and is remembered by the regiments' surgeon to have gone on moving her pots and sacks from whichever corner the fighting had just left.

title: The colonel's report
summary: The first regiment's colonel writes that the column held the bank at Muileann ghlas longer than any force he had faced in two years of war, and sets it down, he says, only so his council should have the field's truth and not a prettier account of it.

title: The taken ground remembered
summary: An old man of Muileann ghlas, brought before the regiments' officers to answer for a store of grain, tells them the field carries an older name, the taken ground, from a battle of the Brothers' War fought on the same ground two centuries before.

title: The sixty come out of the byres
summary: After dark, some sixty of the column still holding the mill and its byres come out under a promise, carried by a Tuathach prisoner on a white cloth, that any man unarmed will be marched and not shot; they are counted, searched and held overnight on the mill floor.

title: The regiments' surgeon treats both sides alike
summary: The regiments' own surgeon, two years out of his training, tends the wounded of both the regiments and the column through the night at Muileann ghlas by two lanterns and a banked fire, and the open record notes that he made no distinction between them.

title: The old man of Cnoc thais brings down his cow
summary: A lame old man of Cnoc thais comes down to the seventh regiment's northernmost post on the Àth leathan road carrying no weapon, leading on a rope halter the one cow his family kept through two summers of war, and is let through with it.

title: The sergeant judges the counting done
summary: At the seventh regiment's northernmost post the sergeant keeping the list of the hills' people notes, when no one more has come down the road by noon, that he takes the empty road to mean the counting is finished.

title: Somhairle hears the guns are done
summary: Somhairle mac Lachlainn hears at the capital, from a clerk who comes into his room without knocking, that the fighting at Muileann ghlas is over; he says afterward that his first thought was for the coal line's timetable and the wounded's carriage north.

title: Somhairle checks the wounded trains twice over
summary: In the first weeks of the peace Somhairle mac Lachlainn has the coal line's schedule for the war's wounded checked twice against the surgeons' own returns, to be sure no man carried north that winter rode on a train meant for other cargo.

title: Near ninety of the column's wounded brought in
summary: The regiments' surgeon's tally for the night after Muileann ghlas stands at twenty-three of the regiments buried or dying and near ninety of the column's wounded brought in.

title: The beacon at Àth dhearg sees no fleet
summary: The keeper of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg on the north-east cape writes in his log through the autumn that no ship of the fleets has passed the cape in three months.
